extracted.intended_audience: citizens/voters of New York and readers evaluating the proposed U.S. Constitution (general public and constitutional critics, 1788)
extracted.subtask_description: A late-18th-century political-legal argument about the proper scope of federal and state taxation powers under the proposed U.S. Constitution, explaining exclusive vs. concurrent authorities and interpreting the Necessary & Proper and Supremacy clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government must possess all powers necessary to its responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: A government ought to contain in itself every power requisite to the full accomplishment of the objects committed to its care, and to the complete execution of the trusts for which it is responsible, free from every other control but a regard to the public good and to the sense of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative rule for constitutional design: when assigning functions to a government, vest it with whatever powers are required to perform those functions effectively, restrained only by public good and popular control. Anti‑pattern: withholding powers necessary for execution and then blaming the government for failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to provide for national defense should be practically unlimited
rubrics_metrics.description: As the duties of superintending the national defense and of securing the public peace against foreign or domestic violence involve a provision for casualties and dangers to which no possible limits can be assigned, the power of making that provision ought to know no other bounds than the exigencies of the nation and the resources of the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: defense-related authorities must be flexible and capacious to meet unforeseeable emergencies. Example: naval preparation for distant commercial protection; policy implication: avoid rigid caps that would incapacitate response to future wars or threats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxation power must enable procurement of revenue for national exigencies
rubrics_metrics.description: As revenue is the essential engine by which the means of answering the national exigencies must be procured, the power of procuring that article in its full extent must necessarily be comprehended in that of providing for those exigencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle linking substantive ends (defense, national needs) to fiscal means: authority to tax follows from the need to fulfill national responsibilities. Scoring note: adequacy of taxation power judged by whether it can fund foreseeable national obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal government requires an unqualified power of taxation (in ordinary modes)
rubrics_metrics.description: As theory and practice conspire to prove that the power of procuring revenue is unavailing when exercised over the States in their collective capacities, the federal government must of necessity be invested with an unqualified power of taxation in the ordinary modes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument for direct federal taxing authority (rather than relying on states): without independent taxing power, the Union cannot reliably meet national needs. Anti‑pattern: expecting states collectively to supply federal revenue in lieu of federal taxing authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: States should retain independent authority to raise revenues (except duties on imports/exports)
rubrics_metrics.description: The individual States should possess an independent and uncontrollable authority to raise their own revenues for the supply of their own wants... under the plan of the convention, they would, with the sole exception of duties on imports and exports, retain that authority in the most absolute and unqualified sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concession intended to reassure: concurrent federal powers coexist with robust state fiscal autonomy except where Constitution expressly restricts states (e.g., import/export duties). Practical implication: evaluate whether proposed federal powers leave states ample revenue means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive delegation arises only in three specific cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusive delegation (alienation of State sovereignty) would only exist in three cases: where the Constitution in express terms granted an exclusive authority to the Union; where it granted in one instance an authority to the Union, and in another prohibited the States from exercising the like authority; and where it granted an authority to the Union to which a similar authority in the States would be absolutely and totally contradictory and repugnant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive test for exclusivity: apply these three criteria to determine whether an authority is exclusive to the Union. Examples provided: exclusive legislation over the federal district; duties on imports/exports (with textual qualifications); uniform rule of naturalization (would be contradictory if states had distinct rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxation of articles (other than exports/imports) is concurrent/coequal
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of imposing taxes on all articles other than exports and imports ... is manifestly a concurrent and coequal authority in the United States and in the individual States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: absent express exclusivity, both federal and state governments may tax the same objects. Practical note: concurrence may produce policy tension, but constitutional structure contemplates mutual prudence and reciprocal forbearance rather than exclusive preemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictive clause regarding imports/exports implies states' powers elsewhere (negative pregnant)
rubrics_metrics.description: The restriction [that 'no State shall, without the consent of Congress, lay any imposts or duties on imports or exports'] amounts to what lawyers call a negative pregnant ... a negation of the authority of the States to impose taxes on imports and exports, and an affirmance of their authority to impose them on all other articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive maxim: a prohibition in one area can imply affirmation in others; do not construe a prohibitory clause so broadly as to produce absurd conclusions (e.g., that states could tax imports with federal consent only).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional repugnancy (direct contradiction) is required to extinguish state authority
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not a mere possibility of inconvenience in the exercise of powers, but an immediate constitutional repugnancy that can by implication alienate and extinguish a pre-existing right of sovereignty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard of implied exclusion: only when a state exercise would be directly contradictory or repugnant to an express federal grant does the state right fall. Practical test: ask whether concurrent exercise would produce an impossible or direct constitutional contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residuary authorities remain with the States unless explicitly divested
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule that all authorities, of which the States are not explicitly divested in favor of the Union, remain with them in full vigor ... is clearly admitted by the whole tenor of the instrument which contains the articles of the proposed Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive presumption: retain state powers by default unless Constitution explicitly removes them. Evidence: insertion of negative clauses in Article I, Section 10 demonstrates convention's care to withhold specific powers from states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary and Proper clause is declaratory of implied means for executing granted powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The clause ... authorizes the national legislature 'to make all laws which shall be NECESSARY and PROPER for carrying into execution THE POWERS by that Constitution vested ...' They are only declaratory of a truth which would have resulted by necessary and unavoidable implication from the very act of constituting a federal government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: the Necessary & Proper clause simply recognizes that a granted legislative power includes the means (laws) necessary to execute it. Anti‑pattern: treating the clause as creating entirely new powers rather than confirming implied means for executing enumerated powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: National government is first judge of necessity; people are ultimate check
rubrics_metrics.description: Who is to judge of the NECESSITY and PROPRIETY of the laws to be passed for executing the powers of the Union? ... the national government, like every other, must judge, in the first instance, of the proper exercise of its powers, and its constituents in the last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocation of interpretive roles: allow the government latitude to decide initially how to execute powers while preserving popular remedies (appeal to the people) for abuses. Example remedies: political redress, constitutional appeal, popular measures to correct usurpation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supremacy applies only to laws made pursuant to the Constitution; unconstitutional acts are usurpations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution and the laws of the United States made IN PURSUANCE THEREOF ... shall be the SUPREME LAW of the land ... though a law, therefore, laying a tax for the use of the United States would be supreme in its nature ... a law for abrogating or preventing the collection of a tax laid by the authority of the State ... would not be the supreme law of the land, but a usurpation of power not granted by the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive limit on supremacy: supremacy vests only in constitutional acts; evaluate whether an act is 'pursuant to' constitutional power before treating it as supreme. Anti‑pattern: assuming every act labeled 'law of the Union' automatically displaces state authority regardless of constitutional basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent jurisdiction reconciles federal capacity and state autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: A CONCURRENT JURISDICTION in the article of taxation was the only admissible substitute for an entire subordination, in respect to this branch of power, of State authority to that of the Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy conclusion: concurrent taxation preserves federal ability to meet national demands while leaving states enough fiscal means for local needs. Supporting arguments: comparative magnitude of federal vs state expenditures, future contingencies argue against exclusive state revenue sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutions must provide capacity for future contingencies; avoid limiting powers to present needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutions of civil government are not to be framed upon a calculation of existing exigencies, but upon a combination of these with the probable exigencies of ages ... There ought to be a CAPACITY to provide for future contingencies as they may happen; and as these are illimitable in their nature, it is impossible safely to limit that capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design principle: when judging the proper scope of powers, account for unforeseeable future threats (e.g., wars, naval needs, shifting international conflicts). Anti‑pattern: restricting constitutional powers to current, immediate calculations of need.
